prompt.context_jp: 富士山のふもとに広がる富士浅田市___、観光地の華やかさから少しだけ外れた、ごく普通の地方都市である。
prompt.prompt_jp: 富士山のふもとに広がる富士浅田市___、観光地の華やかさから少しだけ外れた、ごく普通の地方都市である。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle. The sentence introduces Fujiasada City as the topic and gives a general description.

feedback.correct_en: The narrator is setting up Fujiasada City as the topic of the entire story and describing what kind of place it is. は fits this 'as for X, it is Y' framing in opening narration.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would present the city as newly identified information answering 'which city?' — but nothing is being distinguished or selected here; the city is simply being introduced as the stage.

contrast_examples.jp: 富士浅田市は普通の地方都市だ。
contrast_examples.en: Fujiasada City is an ordinary regional city. (describing the topic)
That is Fujiasada City. (identifying which city)

prompt.context_jp: そのささやかな日常のなかに、宇宙人という途方もない秘密___交ざり始めていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: そのささやかな日常のなかに、宇宙人という途方もない秘密___交ざり始めていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle. The 'incredible secret' is being introduced for the first time into the scene.

feedback.correct_en: This sentence drops a brand-new element — the alien secret — into the already-established daily life. が marks that fresh, previously-unmentioned subject appearing on stage.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would treat the secret as already-known topic. But the whole dramatic point is that this is a startling new intrusion into the ordinary.

contrast_examples.en: A secret began to mix in. (new element appears)

contrast_examples.jp: その秘密は、誰も知らない。
contrast_examples.en: That secret, no one knows about. (secret already in play)

prompt.context_jp: その秘密___ 幼なじみの はっちと みなぷーしか知らない
prompt.prompt_jp: その秘密___ 幼なじみの はっちと みなぷーしか知らない
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle. 'That secret' was mentioned in the previous sentence.

feedback.correct_en: 'That secret' is already in play (just introduced). The sentence comments on it: 'as for that secret, only Hacchi and Minapu know it.' は carries this topic-continuation.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would make the secret sound newly identified, as if answering 'which thing do only they know?' — but the secret is already the shared referent.

contrast_examples.jp: その秘密は二人しか知らない。
contrast_examples.en: As for that secret, only two people know. (comment on known topic)
There's a secret. (introducing it fresh)

prompt.context_jp: そんな中…今日 清美たちを脅かす新たな男___ この町に降り立つ
prompt.prompt_jp: 今日 清美たちを脅かす新たな男___ この町に降り立つ
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle. A 'new man' is about to appear in the story for the first time.

feedback.correct_en: A 'new man who threatens them' is being introduced as a fresh dramatic entry — classic が for a newly arriving referent. The chapter title itself (よそ者、町に降り立つ) frames him as a stranger making his first appearance.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would presuppose the man as a known topic, but he has not been mentioned yet; the point is his arrival.

contrast_examples.en: A new man appeared. (new entry)
That man is dangerous. (already known)

prompt.context_jp: この辺り___観光ルートから外れているぶん、素通りされがちな地域だった。
prompt.prompt_jp: この辺り___観光ルートから外れているぶん、素通りされがちな地域だった。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle. The narrator is characterizing 'this area' as a topic.

feedback.correct_en: The sentence takes 'this area' as its topic and describes a general property of it. は is the natural choice for this kind of generic characterization.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would pick 'this area' out as newly distinguished among options, but no selection is happening — the narrator is simply explaining what kind of area it is.

contrast_examples.en: This area is quiet. (describing the area)

contrast_examples.jp: この辺りが一番静かだ。
contrast_examples.en: This area is the quietest. (singling it out)

prompt.context_jp: 富士浅田の懐の深さを、彼___まだ知らずにいた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 富士浅田の懐の深さを、彼___まだ知らずにいた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle. 'He' (Matsuzaki, an outsider) is being contrasted with those who know the town.

feedback.correct_en: 'He' is the topic being commented on, with an implicit contrast: others may sense the town's depth, but he does not yet. は carries both topic and that contrastive nuance.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would present 'he' as a newly identified subject answering 'who doesn't know?' — but the focus is the comment about him, not identifying him.

contrast_examples.en: He doesn't know yet. (topic/contrast)
It was HE who didn't know. (identifying)

prompt.context_jp: 岸本___資料の細部に集中する癖があり、こうした小さな確認を怠らない。
prompt.prompt_jp: 岸本___資料の細部に集中する癖があり、こうした小さな確認を怠らない。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle. The narrator describes Kishimoto's general habit.

feedback.correct_en: This is a character-establishing comment about Kishimoto's habitual behavior. は takes him as topic and gives a general trait.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would feel like answering 'who has this habit?' — but no such question is implicit; it's a direct description of him.

contrast_examples.en: He is a meticulous person. (characterization)
He was the one who noticed. (identifying who)

prompt.context_jp: 遅れて入り口に姿を見せたの___、清美と幼なじみの三人組だった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 遅れて入り口に姿を見せたの___、清美と幼なじみの三人組だった。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle in this cleft sentence identifying who appeared.

feedback.correct_en: This is a のは…だった cleft that singles out and identifies the referent. The は here sets up the identifying frame: 'the ones who appeared were X.'
feedback.incorrect_en: が doesn't work with the のXだった cleft structure; the のは…だった pattern is fixed.

contrast_examples.en: The one who came was my friend. (cleft)
A friend came. (plain new-info)

prompt.context_jp: ドリンクバーの角氷___、グラスの中で小さく崩れる音がした。
prompt.prompt_jp: ドリンクバーの角氷___、グラスの中で小さく崩れる音がした。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle. A sensory detail — ice in a glass — is being introduced into the scene.

feedback.correct_en: The ice is a freshly observed sensory event — the narrator is pulling it in as a new scene detail. が marks this neutral description of something perceived.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would frame the ice as a known topic to comment on, but the sentence is painting an atmospheric moment, not continuing talk about ice.

contrast_examples.en: There was the sound of ice cracking. (neutral event)
That ice had melted. (comment on known ice)

prompt.context_jp: 別のテーブルでは、松崎___幼い女の子を連れた母親にマイクを向けていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 別のテーブルでは、松崎___幼い女の子を連れた母親にマイクを向けていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle. The narrative camera cuts to a different table and shows Matsuzaki in action.

feedback.correct_en: This is a scene-cut: '別のテーブルでは' sets the location, and が neutrally reports what is happening there — Matsuzaki is observed in the act. Subordinate-like perceptual description favors が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would elevate Matsuzaki to the sentence topic, but this sentence is painting a scene, not making a comment about him as a known topic in this stretch of the chapter.

contrast_examples.jp: 向こうでは子供が遊んでいた。
contrast_examples.en: Over there, children were playing. (scene description)
Matsuzaki is a cameraman. (comment on topic)

prompt.context_jp: 昼休みに偶然見つけた、その小さな金属片___、彼女の手のひらの中で鈍く光っている。
prompt.prompt_jp: 昼休みに偶然見つけた、その小さな金属片___、彼女の手のひらの中で鈍く光っている。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle. The 'small metal piece' was just introduced in the previous sentence (the bent coin).

feedback.correct_en: The coin was just introduced; this sentence continues talking about it as the established topic ('that small metal piece — it glows dully...'). は signals topic continuation.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would introduce the coin as newly appearing information, but it's already in the reader's attention from the preceding sentence.

contrast_examples.jp: その金属片は手の中で光っていた。
contrast_examples.en: That metal piece was glowing in her hand. (continuing topic)

contrast_examples.jp: 手の中で何かが光った。
contrast_examples.en: Something glowed in her hand. (brand-new element)

prompt.context_jp: フロントの奥から、ちょうど高橋孝介___姿を見せた。
prompt.prompt_jp: フロントの奥から、ちょうど高橋孝介___姿を見せた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle. Takahashi appears on-stage at just the right moment.

feedback.correct_en: This is a classic 'enter stage' moment — Takahashi walks into view. が reports the appearance neutrally as a fresh event in the scene.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would make it sound like we were already discussing Takahashi and are now commenting on him; but the sentence is announcing his entry.

contrast_examples.jp: ドアから人が入ってきた。
contrast_examples.en: Someone came in through the door. (appearance event)
That person was Takahashi. (identifying known referent)

prompt.context_jp: 高橋の顔から、一瞬だけ表情___抜け落ちた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 高橋の顔から、一瞬だけ表情___抜け落ちた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle. A visible change on his face is being described.

feedback.correct_en: A sudden observed change ('his expression dropped for a moment') is a neutral descriptive event — が marks the subject of such a perceptual report.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would set 'expression' up as a topic to comment on generally, but this is a one-time momentary observation.

contrast_examples.en: The expression vanished. (observed event)

contrast_examples.jp: 彼の表情はいつも穏やかだ。
contrast_examples.en: His expression is always calm. (general trait)

prompt.context_jp: 拡大された写真の中に、明らかな橙色の点___浮かび上がっていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 拡大された写真の中に、明らかな橙色の点___浮かび上がっていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle. The orange dot is noticed in the photo for the first time.

feedback.correct_en: The orange dot is a newly discovered detail inside the enlarged image — が introduces this fresh perceptual find that drives the plot connection.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would presuppose the dot as a known referent, but the whole point is that they are just now spotting it.

contrast_examples.jp: 写真に何かが写っていた。
contrast_examples.en: Something was captured in the photo. (new discovery)
That dot was small. (comment on already-known dot)

prompt.context_jp: 繁盛してほしいか、静かなままでいてほしいか、どちらかしかない、というほど単純な二択ではないと清美___思う。
prompt.prompt_jp: ...というほど単純な二択ではないと清美___思う。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle. Kiyomi is being presented as the one who holds this thought.

feedback.correct_en: Kiyomi is the known topic of this stretch of narrative; the sentence comments on what she thinks. は carries topic continuation.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would single her out as 'the one who thinks' versus others, which isn't the contrast at play here.

contrast_examples.en: She thinks it's different. (comment on topic)
She was the one who objected. (identifying who)

prompt.context_jp: ローカルの空気に触れてから決めるほうが早い、というのが彼の____だった。
prompt.prompt_jp: ローカルの空気に触れてから決めるほうが早い、というのが彼の____だった。
prompt.prompt_en: Fill the blank. The sentence describes Kishimoto's personal working style/way of doing things.

feedback.correct_en: 流儀 means 'one's own way/style of doing things,' which perfectly describes Kishimoto's personal method of judging only after soaking in the local atmosphere.
feedback.incorrect_en: 流行 is 'trend/fashion,' 流れ is 'flow/current,' and 流通 is 'distribution/circulation' — none describe a personal working style.

contrast_examples.en: That is his way of doing things.
It's the current trend.

prompt.context_jp: 岸本は資料の細部に集中する癖があり、こうした小さな確認を____。
prompt.prompt_jp: 岸本は...こうした小さな確認を____。
prompt.prompt_en: Fill the blank. Kishimoto is described as never neglecting small checks.

feedback.correct_en: 確認を怠らない ('never neglect to confirm') is a fixed collocation describing a conscientious habit. It fits his meticulous character perfectly.
feedback.incorrect_en: 許さない ('not allow') makes no sense with 確認を; 終わらない and 離れない don't collocate with 確認 to mean 'doesn't neglect.'

contrast_examples.en: Never neglect preparation.
To be careless / neglect caution.

prompt.context_jp: 古い雑居ビルの一角にある小さな店で、常連しか知らないはずの____である。
prompt.prompt_jp: 常連しか知らないはずの____である。
prompt.prompt_en: Fill the blank. A small shop known only to regulars — what kind of place?

feedback.correct_en: 隠れ家 ('hideaway, hidden gem') is the standard word for a tucked-away café/shop that only insiders know. It matches '常連しか知らない' exactly.
feedback.incorrect_en: 住まい is a residence, 本店 is a 'main branch,' and 空き家 is a vacant house — none describe a secret in-the-know spot.

contrast_examples.en: A hideaway only for regulars.
This is the main branch.

prompt.context_jp: 早めに来て正解だった、という____が三人のあいだを行き来する。
prompt.prompt_jp: 早めに来て正解だった、という____が三人のあいだを行き来する。
prompt.prompt_en: Fill the blank. The three friends feel relieved they came early.

feedback.correct_en: 安堵 means 'relief,' which matches '早めに来て正解だった' — being glad they came early and avoided the line.
feedback.incorrect_en: 不安 (anxiety), 緊張 (tension), 後悔 (regret) all contradict the feeling of 'good thing we came early.'

contrast_examples.en: To let out a sigh of relief.
Anxiety crosses one's mind.

prompt.context_jp: いや いちやまのお惣菜 ____ないほうがいいよ
prompt.prompt_jp: いちやまのお惣菜 ____ないほうがいいよ
prompt.prompt_en: Fill the blank. 'You shouldn't ___ Ichiyama's side dishes' — meaning don't underestimate them.

feedback.correct_en: ナメる (lit. 'to lick') is slangy for 'to underestimate / look down on.' 'ナメないほうがいい' means 'don't underestimate them' — the deli at Ichiyama is surprisingly good.
feedback.incorrect_en: 'Don't eat/don't buy/don't touch' would all reverse or miss the speaker's praise. The whole line is defending the deli.

contrast_examples.jp: この店をナメないほうがいい。
contrast_examples.en: Don't underestimate this shop.
Don't look down on your opponent.

prompt.context_jp: 考え始めれば、簡単には離れられない類の____だった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 考え始めれば、簡単には離れられない類の____だった。
prompt.prompt_en: Fill the blank. The bent coin is 'the kind of ___ that you can't easily let go of.'

feedback.correct_en: 代物 ('item/piece of work,' often with a hint of being peculiar) fits a mysterious physical object. '〜類の代物' is a common pattern meaning 'the kind of thing that...'
feedback.incorrect_en: 人物 is a person, 名物 is a famous local product, 見物 is a sight-seeing spectacle — none fit a mysterious coin in one's hand.

contrast_examples.en: It's a troublesome piece of work.
He's a famous person.

prompt.context_jp: 真実からは、____なほど遠ざかっていくやりとりだった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 真実からは、____なほど遠ざかっていくやりとりだった。
prompt.prompt_en: Fill the blank. They're guessing Onodera is the culprit, but Takahashi actually did it — their conversation drifts away from the truth.

feedback.correct_en: 皮肉 means 'ironic.' The characters are earnestly closing in on a 'suspect,' but ironically moving further from the real answer. 皮肉なほど ('ironically so') captures this narrator's wry commentary.
feedback.incorrect_en: 正直 (honest), 親切 (kind), 新鮮 (fresh) don't match the narrator's dry observation about dramatic irony.

contrast_examples.en: It ended with an ironic result.
To say honestly.

prompt.context_jp: 休日の午後を丸ごと友人に付き合う日は、社会人になってからだんだんと____になっていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: ...だんだんと____になっていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Fill the blank. Spending a whole holiday afternoon with friends — what does it become once you start working?

feedback.correct_en: 貴重 ('precious, rare') captures the nostalgic note: once you're a working adult, free time with friends becomes something precious.
feedback.incorrect_en: 退屈 (boring), 簡単 (easy), 正確 (accurate) don't fit the wistful tone of describing time with friends.

contrast_examples.en: Precious time.
Boring time.

prompt.context_jp: A new 'outsider' is about to arrive and threaten the main cast. Which phrasing lands more naturally as a dramatic chapter-closing line in Japanese narration?
prompt.prompt_en: Which version is more natural as the dramatic closing line of the chapter opener?

choices.text: 今日 清美たちを脅かす新たな男が この町に降り立つ
今日 新たな男が 清美たちを脅かすために この町に降り立つ

feedback.correct_en: Option A reads with the compact, pre-nominal modifier '清美たちを脅かす新たな男' — standard Japanese narrative compression. It lands with impact as a cliffhanger.
feedback.incorrect_en: Option B unpacks the modifier into a 〜ために purpose clause, which is grammatical but reads as awkward exposition rather than tense narration.

contrast_examples.en: A man who is after him appears. (compressed modifier)

contrast_examples.jp: 一人の男が、彼を狙うために現れる。
contrast_examples.en: A man appears in order to go after him. (unpacked, feels explanatory)

prompt.context_jp: The three friends realize the café is packed and decide to leave. Which short exchange sounds more natural in casual spoken Japanese among close friends?
prompt.prompt_en: Which exchange sounds more natural between close friends deciding to leave a crowded café?

choices.text: 「どうする？ 出る？」「出ますかね」
「どうしますか？ 退出しましょうか？」「はい、退出いたしましょう」

feedback.correct_en: A is the casual, friend-group register of the chapter: short, elliptical, ending-particle ね softens the decision. It matches how Kiyomi and friends actually talk.
feedback.incorrect_en: B uses 退出 and 〜いたしましょう — business/formal keigo totally out of place among childhood friends in a café.

contrast_examples.en: Shall we head out? (casual)

contrast_examples.jp: 恐れ入りますが、退出させていただきます。
contrast_examples.en: Excuse me, I'll be taking my leave. (formal/business)

prompt.context_jp: A truck driver tells a strange teleportation story and adds that no one believes him. Which casual self-deprecating line sounds more natural?
prompt.prompt_en: Which line sounds more natural in casual conversation after an unbelievable story?

choices.text: まあ 誰に話しても 信じてくれないんだけど
まあ 誰に話しても 信じられないのです

feedback.correct_en: A uses 信じてくれない (literally 'won't believe me for me') + the softening 〜んだけど tail, which is exactly how a casual speaker frames a self-aware aside.
feedback.incorrect_en: B's 信じられないのです is stiff, written-sounding, and shifts the meaning toward '(I) can't believe it' rather than 'they won't believe me.' It clashes with the chatty tone.

contrast_examples.jp: 信じてくれないんだけどね。
contrast_examples.en: They won't believe me, though. (casual aside)

contrast_examples.jp: 彼は信じられない人物です。
contrast_examples.en: He is an unbelievable person. (formal/different meaning)

prompt.context_jp: Kiyomi silently warns Takahashi with just a look not to say anything incriminating. Which narration reads more naturally?
prompt.prompt_en: Which narrative version flows more naturally in literary Japanese?

choices.text: 清美は、彼が余計なことを口走らないよう、視線だけで釘を刺した。
清美は視線だけで釘を刺した、彼が余計なことを口走らないように。

feedback.correct_en: A places the purpose clause 〜ないよう before the main verb — standard Japanese order where modifiers precede what they modify. It flows naturally.
feedback.incorrect_en: B dangles the purpose clause after the verb as an afterthought, which reads as English-style syntax and feels unnatural in Japanese prose.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼女は遅れないよう早く出た。
contrast_examples.en: She left early so as not to be late. (natural order)

contrast_examples.jp: 彼女は早く出た、遅れないように。
contrast_examples.en: She left early, so as not to be late. (awkward trailing clause)
